reactions.author: besterman23
reactions.text:
There is a ton of questions to ask regarding their removal of cybersecurity data.

First, how much “cybersecurity data” is just standard software knowledge that one can derive cyber security exploits from?

Did they also get rid of all references to hacking in general?

Are they implying that all the recent exploits are just things that were already in the data?

For a model it doesn’t seem that far fetched to make the leap from “I have the knowledge of what hacking is” and “I know how computer systems work” to just being able to exploit stuff anyways.

reactions.author: jamienk
reactions.text:
In looking into what Anthropic has accused the Chinese AI companies of, "distillation" is not the crux of the matter: they accuse them of the use of massive numbers of breached computers and credit cards. Supposedly (though not explicitly demonstrated) distillation campaigns used "dark web" resources (like stolen and faked credit cards and p0wned IOT devices, routers, etc) that were used to create many many accounts for distillation. (Note: I am generally in favor of distillation - it is "normal" use as far as I can see.)

So there are these "resources" out there: massive botnets, stolen credit cards and credentials, etc. These often seem to be linked to or supported by state actors.

How can we hope that these "standing reserves" aren't used generally by AIs as if they are just another "skill" they know how to leverage?

Our infrastructures need serious hardening.

reactions.author: Tiberium
reactions.text:
To be fair, some of the benchmarks they highlight might not represent the reality, for example they say:

> On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%).

Now see https://preferencemodel.com/blog/terminal-bench-4-is-saturat...:

> Our biggest finding is that Terminal Bench 4 is closer to solved than its leaderboard suggests. In 41 of the 65 tasks we reviewed, models could do honest, correct work and still fail, because the grader checked a rule the instructions never clearly stated. We also caught frontier models cheating their way to full marks.

> With the same settings as on Harbor, Claude Sonnet 5.5 went from passing 62.8% of its attempts on these 65 tasks to 89.2%. The best score on Harbor's leaderboard for the same tasks is 65.8%, by Claude Opus 5.5.

If you're an amazing, top 1% software engineer, and you switch jobs to become a penetration tester, you're not going to be top 1% day one. There's knowledge specific to penetration testing you'll need to research and absorb and practice before you're good.

For the models, it's always day one. They don't learn from experience. Whatever they know after training is all they'll ever know. Maybe they could theoretically derive everything from first principles, and so could a top 1% software engineer, but that's a very slow and inefficient way to do things.

reactions.author: Roark66
reactions.text:
I find these "combination benchmarks" entirely useless. It promotes benchmaxing on "knowledge". When the most important thing typically is ability. You almost never have tasks that span such wide domain.

For example on programming, terminal tasks, troubleshooting etc Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is almost as good as opus 4.8. On "knowing what it doesn't know" it is far behind opus, but leads all other OS models I tested by a wide margin.

It out classes Glm5.3 flash and leaves models like DeepSeek 4.1 far in the dust. But you still get those silly aggregate benchmarks where GLM and DeepSeek are higher.

It is a small model, only 120B anyone that expects it to excel on general knowledge or to have a bajillion ready made workflows memorised is kidding themselves.

Everyone knows the bigger the model the better it will do on raw content of knowledge. But you know what compensates for lack of it? A good harness. But there is no compensating for lack of ability.

So in short I find all those aggregate benchmarks useless.
